title: Almighty (CCC 268–278)
hookLine: God shows his almighty power most of all in mercy

lines: A WEIGHTLIFTER. A STORM. A FIST.
A MAN TYING A TODDLER'S SHOE.
cards: What does strength look like? A weightlifter with the bar overhead. A storm that peels a roof off.
A fist on a table. Now another scene: a big man down on one knee on a sidewalk, tying a toddler's shoe, careful not to pull the laces too tight. That's strength too, the kind that holds itself back.
The Creed calls God the Father almighty, and when the Catechism explains that word, it makes a claim about where that power shows most. Today's word: almighty.

teach.h: MERCY UPON ALL, FOR THOU CANST DO ALL.
teach.b: Almighty means able to do all things. Mary sings it in Luke's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "he that is mighty, hath done great things to me."
But the Book of Wisdom ties that power to something unexpected, saying to God: "thou hast mercy upon all, because thou canst do all things." Mercy because of power, not in spite of it.
The Catechism pairs the Creed's two words, Father and almighty, and says they shed light on each other: a father's power, never arbitrary, never a whim.

Then it faces the hard question that day two hundred ninety-nine called why evil. If God is almighty, why so much suffering? The Catechism admits that faith in God's power can be put to the test by evil.

teach.h: THE CROSS: THE POWER OF GOD.
teach.b: Its answer points to the cross, where God looks weakest; Paul calls the crucified Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.
The Catechism says God shows his almighty power by turning people from their sins and bringing them back to friendship with him.
And it quotes a prayer of the Roman Mass that goes further: God shows his almighty power most of all by sparing and by showing mercy.
On this reading, any force can break things; it takes a deeper power to forgive, and to heal what's broken. The Creed's first adjective isn't a threat hanging over the world.
It's the strength of someone who can afford to be gentle.

how: Catholics profess God as the Father almighty in the Creed at Mass, and some of the Church's prayers, including the one the Catechism quotes, address God's power and his mercy together.

o: deciding every outcome on a passing whim
ruling by force, whatever anyone wants
able to do all things, shown most in mercy

p: mercy upon all, because God can do all
the power of God, says Paul
power shown most in sparing and mercy

s: the Catechism says God's power is arbitrary
it says it's never arbitrary, and it's joined to his fatherhood.
the Catechism avoids the question of suffering
it admits evil can test faith in God's power, and points to the cross.
a prayer the Catechism quotes says God shows his power most by sparing and showing mercy

games.q: the Catechism quotes a prayer of the Mass on how God shows his almighty power most of all. what does it say?
games.why: most of all by sparing and showing mercy. the Catechism adds that God shows his power by turning people from their sins and back to friendship with him.

practice: Think of a moment coming up today when you'll hold a little power: over a child, a coworker who made a mistake, someone on a customer service line, a slow driver ahead of you.
Picture it clearly, then picture using that power gently, a softer word, a little patience, a small offense let go, and rehearse it once, start to finish.
If you pray, ask God for that kind of strength; if you don't, just hold the picture steady.

wordCard.voice: Almighty. Able to do all things, and, in the Catechism's reading, showing that power above all in mercy and forgiveness. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: the word the Greek creeds use where English says almighty.

carryVoice: Your line: power as mercy. Like a big man kneeling to tie a small shoe. See you tomorrow.
